residencyRequirements.description: If the grounds for divorce occurred outside Maryland, at least one party must have been a resident of Maryland for at least 6 months before filing. If the grounds occurred in Maryland, the filing party need only be a current resident — no minimum period is required.

exceptions: Mutual consent divorces have no waiting period; 6-month separation ground requires 6 months of living separate and apart before filing
waitingPeriod.description: Maryland has no post-filing waiting period for mutual consent divorces. For the separation ground, the parties must have lived separate and apart without cohabitation for at least 6 months before filing.

noFault.name: Mutual Consent
noFault.description: Both parties consent to the divorce and submit a written settlement agreement resolving all issues. No waiting period required. Both parties must appear at the hearing.

noFault.name: Irreconcilable Differences
noFault.description: The differences between the parties are irreconcilable and there is no reasonable prospect of reconciliation. No separation period required. Added effective October 1, 2023.

noFault.name: 6-Month Separation
noFault.description: The parties have lived separate and apart for at least 6 months before filing. Under the October 2023 amendments, spouses may be considered 'separate' while living under the same roof if they pursue separate lives.

groundsForDivorce.notes: Effective October 1, 2023 (HB 380), Maryland eliminated ALL fault-based grounds for divorce (adultery, desertion, conviction, insanity, cruelty). Maryland is now a purely no-fault state. Mutual consent is the fastest path — no waiting period and no separation required, but both parties must agree and sign a written settlement agreement. The irreconcilable differences ground also requires no separation. The 6-month separation ground requires living apart (parties may live under the same roof if they 'pursue separate lives') for at least 6 months before filing.

propertyDivision.description: Maryland divides marital property equitably, considering each spouse's contributions (monetary and non-monetary), the value of property, the economic circumstances of each spouse, how and when property was acquired, and any award of alimony. The court may grant a monetary award to achieve equity but generally does not transfer title to property.
propertyDivision.separateProperty: Property acquired before marriage or by gift or inheritance during marriage is non-marital (separate) property and is not subject to equitable distribution, unless it has been commingled.

filingFees.notes: Maryland filing fees for absolute divorce are approximately $165 but may vary by county. Fee waivers are available for qualifying low-income individuals via Md. Rule 1-325.

basic.name: Financial Statement
basic.description: Disclosure of income, assets, and debts (required in contested cases and when alimony or child support is sought)

basic.name: Judgment of Absolute Divorce
basic.description: Final court order dissolving the marriage

service.name: Acceptance of Service
service.notes: Must be signed by defendant and filed with the court

withChildren.name: Child Support Guidelines Worksheet
withChildren.description: Income shares calculation per Md. Code, Fam. Law § 12-204

inState.description: Defendant must file a response within 30 days of service

outOfState.description: Defendant served outside Maryland must file a response within 60 days of service

childSupportGuidelines.description: Maryland uses an income shares model. Both parents' adjusted actual incomes are combined and the child support obligation is determined from a schedule based on the combined monthly adjusted actual income and the number of children.
childSupportGuidelines.notes: The court may deviate from the guidelines if application would be unjust or inappropriate in a particular case.

maintenanceGuidelines.description: Maryland courts may award rehabilitative alimony (for a set period to allow the recipient to become self-supporting), indefinite alimony (when the party cannot reasonably be expected to become self-supporting or when the difference in living standards would be unconscionably disparate), or pendente lite alimony (temporary support during the proceeding). There are no statutory formulas — the court exercises broad discretion.
maintenanceGuidelines.eligibility: Any spouse may seek alimony from the other. The court considers the factors in Md. Code, Fam. Law § 11-106(b), including each party's financial needs and resources, the standard of living during marriage, the duration of the marriage, contributions, and the circumstances that contributed to the estrangement.

court.name: Circuit Court
court.description: Divorce cases in Maryland are filed in the Circuit Court for the county (or Baltimore City) where either party resides.
